imageInfo.caption: Louis VII, crowned and on horseback, receives a plea from the patriarch of Jerusalem in the Grandes Chroniques de France illuminated for Charles V in about 1375–1380.
imageInfo.creator: Unknown Parisian illuminator
imageInfo.source: Wikimedia Commons (Gallica, Bibliothèque nationale de France), public domain
imageInfo.note: Miniature from the copy of the Grandes Chroniques de France made for Charles V, Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 2813, fol. 216v. The BnF title reads "Louis VII supplié par Foucher, patriarche de Jérusalem": the kneeling churchman with the patriarchal cross hands the king a letter. It was painted about two centuries after Louis died in 1180, so his fleur-de-lis armour and crown are those of the 1370s. It is not a likeness. His seal of about 1137 to 1180 is the only image of him made in his lifetime.

overview: Louis VII was king of France and one of the royal leaders of the Second Crusade. His failed eastern expedition and annulment from Eleanor of Aquitaine reshaped Capetian and Angevin politics.
His legacy combines piety, crusading failure, and the dynastic consequences of losing Aquitaine to the Angevin world.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Louis VII was king of France and one of the royal leaders of the Second Crusade. His failed eastern expedition and annulment from Eleanor of Aquitaine reshaped Capetian and Angevin politics.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Louis was raised for church life before his elder brother’s death made him heir, a background that influenced his piety and kingship.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Louis VII of France is remembered as a pious, well-meaning, and somewhat ineffectual king, whose monastic temperament sat awkwardly on a throne that demanded harder qualities. The sources present a ruler of genuine and conventional devotion — he had been intended for the church before his brother's death made him heir — whose religious scruples and mild nature contrasted with the political ruthlessness of his rivals and successors.

His leadership of the Second Crusade was earnest but unsuccessful, and his marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine ended in an annulment that proved a political disaster, since she promptly married Henry of Anjou and carried her vast lands into the Angevin camp. The chroniclers, even sympathetic ones, convey a king better suited to prayer than to the cynical contest of twelfth-century power politics.

What the record supports is a decent, devout, and patient ruler whose virtues were personal rather than political, and who was repeatedly outmaneuvered by tougher opponents. He is remembered as the pious king whose gentleness and miscalculations — above all the loss of Eleanor and Aquitaine — shaped the long Capetian-Angevin struggle more through failure than through strength.

contentSections.title: As crusader king of France
paragraphs: Louis took the cross after the fall of Edessa and traveled east with Eleanor. The campaign suffered in Anatolia and failed before Damascus, weakening royal prestige and contributing to marital and political rupture.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Louis died in 1180, leaving a strengthened Capetian succession through Philip II despite the earlier loss of Aquitaine through Eleanor’s remarriage.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His legacy combines piety, crusading failure, and the dynastic consequences of losing Aquitaine to the Angevin world.
